title: Pressure and choking: why easy targets get missed
summary: Under pressure, skilled shooters sometimes start steering a shot they usually make without thinking. How to spot the signs and what can help.

body.html: Choking means shooting clearly below your usual level because of pressure. One common explanation: under pressure you start checking, step by step, a skill that normally runs on its own, and that disrupts it.
Worry also pulls attention away from the target. Under anxiety, attention is drawn to worrying thoughts and threats, so less of it is left for the task.
Signs you can notice on the stand:

html: Your tempo changes: you rush the call, or stand too long.
You consciously check the gun mount or the swing.
Your eyes go to the barrel or the bead instead of the target.
You keep looking at the scores or at your rivals.
Your grip and shoulders get tighter.
You miss targets that are usually easy for you.

body.html: What can help: your usual routine and tempo, and one simple cue about the target. A review of 47 studies on choking found that a routine and one simple cue word for the whole shot are among the things that help. More in Pre-shot routine: the same steps in the same order and Cue words and self-talk.
Process goals keep your mind on what you do rather than on the result: see Process goals and the score.

Training under mild pressure that grows step by step can prepare you for the real thing. Examples: “five in a row”, a scored practice round, a practice shoot-off, a few spectators, a time limit. More in Training for competition.

A skill you learned mostly by doing, without many spoken rules about elbows and feet, tends to hold up better under pressure. That is one reason many coaches keep technical talk for training and give only short cue words at competitions.
In a shoot-off, keep the same routine and the same tempo. Rushing under pressure has been linked with worse results, for example in football penalties.

If you may be in a shoot-off, stay warm, drink water and stay close. In both disciplines you may have to shoot within 15 minutes of the call (Chapter 18 · Shoot-off squads, call-up and postponement, Chapter 14 · Staying available for a shoot-off).
Most of this research comes from lab tasks and other sports, not from Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ or Compak® Sporting. So it most likely works the same way here too.
If pressure keeps spoiling your competitions over a long time, a sport psychologist can help you build a plan.

notes.html: Raise the pressure in training a little at a time, and stop a pressure drill before technique breaks down. Notice which targets fail first under pressure: they show what to train.

key_points.html: Choking often comes from consciously steering a skill that usually runs on its own.
Signs: a changed tempo, checking the mount, eyes on the bead, watching the scores.
Keep your usual routine, tempo and one simple cue.
Train under pressure that grows step by step.
In a shoot-off: the same routine and the same tempo.

did_you_know.html: Some athletes keep a song running in their head during a competition. In one small study, this kind of distraction helped athletes who tended to choke.

quiz.q: Which is a typical sign of choking on the stand?

options.text: Your tempo stays just as in training
You start consciously checking your mount
You drink a little water between the stands

quiz.explain: Consciously checking a skill that usually runs on its own is a common sign of choking.

quiz.q: What tends to help under pressure?

options.text: Changing your technique on the day itself
Checking the scores after each stand
Your usual routine and one simple cue

quiz.explain: A review of choking studies found that a routine and one simple cue are among the things that help.

quiz.q: How can you shoot a shoot-off?

options.text: With your usual routine and tempo
Faster, to get it over with

quiz.explain: Rushing and over-checking are both signs of pressure; your usual routine and tempo are a good default.
